title: Al-Balad: two eyes, a tongue, two lips
hook: have We not given him two eyes, a tongue and lips, and shown him two ways (90:8–10)
tomorrow: Al-Fajr: the dawn and ten nights

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Balad, and the climb it names: freeing someone, feeding the hungry. Your line was take the steep path.

Try this. Touch your eyelids, gently. Then your lips. Then press your tongue against the back of your teeth. All three have been busy all day, mostly without a thought: reading this screen, talking to the barista, tasting the coffee, muttering at the traffic. Equipment doesn't get more ordinary than this. Right before the steep path, Al-Balad stops and points at exactly this equipment, and asks a question about it. Then it adds one more gift that you can't touch at all.
screen: `TOUCH YOUR EYELIDS. YOUR LIPS.` → `EVERYDAY EQUIPMENT.` → `ONE GIFT YOU CAN'T TOUCH.`

segments.voice: Al-Balad describes a man who boasts that he has spent heaps of money and thinks no one sees him. The surah answers with a question, verse eight, in Pickthall's words: Did We not assign unto him two eyes, and a tongue and two lips? The man who thinks no one sees him was given the power to see. The man bragging with his mouth was given the mouth. It's a gentle, almost funny reversal: everything he's using to show off was handed to him. Why two lips, and not just a mouth? Some commentators notice that lips close. The tongue can speak, and the lips can hold it back; the same equipment can say the cruel thing or keep it in. Then verse ten: and We showed him the two ways. The Arabic is an-najdayn, the two raised roads, the two highland paths. Ibn Kathir gives the common reading: the way of good and the way of harm, both shown clearly, like two roads on a ridge you can see from far off. He also reports a few who read it more tenderly, as the two sources of milk a newborn is guided to without being taught. Either way, guidance was given before you asked for it. Eyes to see the roads, a tongue to speak on the good one, lips to stop at the other. Then verse eleven, from yesterday: but he did not attempt the steep path. So the surah's logic runs: you were given the tools, you were shown the roads, now climb.
screen: `THE ONE WHO THINKS NO ONE SEES.` · `EYES, TONGUE, AND LIPS THAT CLOSE.` · `AN-NAJDAYN — THE TWO RAISED ROADS.` · `GIVEN THE TOOLS, SHOWN THE ROADS.` · then, large: `TWO ROADS SHOWN.`

segments.voice: Rest your attention on your mouth: the tongue resting, the lips closed. Then think of one thing you could say that would help someone, a thank you, an apology, a word of praise to someone who never hears it. Keep the lips closed for now, and just choose the words.
Al-Balad. The city, Surah ninety: eyes, a tongue, two lips, and the two roads shown. Today's word.
Your line: two roads shown. The same tongue can take either one. See you at dawn.

screen: `DAY 194 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AL-FAJR: THE DAWN AND TEN NIGHTS.`

howItsDone: Muslims often recall these verses of Al-Balad when speaking of guarding the tongue, a theme that runs through many hadith, and of gratitude for the senses as gifts that come with responsibility.

fork.reveal: a question, not a lecture: the eyes, tongue and lips he's using were given to him, and so were the two roads.

original.note: Arabic: "the two raised roads," the dual of najd, high ground (Qur'an 90:10).

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of body parts.
what it means: the tools for seeing and speaking were given, and the two roads were shown; the rest is the climb.
what a scholar hears: najd is raised, visible ground, the name of the Arabian plateau too; the dual najdayn means two paths plain to see. a minority reading takes them as a mother's two breasts.
